image.alt: Two panels. Left: a rail station in the middle of a ten-minute walking circle, with shops on the ground floor of apartment and office buildings, a small park and sidewalks, all close together. Right: houses on curving dead-end streets far from a strip mall and an office park, linked only by a wide road.
image.caption: A LevlPrep drawing comparing two neighborhood designs.

table.caption: Two neighborhoods in the same metro area, 2025 (invented data for practice)
rows: Share of trips on foot, bike or transit
Average monthly rent for two bedrooms
Average car kilometers per household per day

items.q: Which feature of the left panel shows mixed-use development?
options: Shops below apartments
The curving dead-end streets lined with houses
The wide road joining the mall and the office park
The strip mall set far away from the homes

why.correct: Mixed use puts homes, shops and offices in the same building or block. Shops below apartments are a classic example.
options: Right: different uses stacked in one building.
Dead-end streets belong to the right panel and separate uses.
A wide road links separated uses; it is not mixed use.
A strip mall far from homes separates uses.

items.q: Which term best describes the design in the left panel?
options: Urban sprawl
An edge city
A squatter settlement
Transit-oriented development

why.correct: Dense, mixed-use building within a short walk of a rail station is transit-oriented development.
options: Sprawl is the low-density, car-based pattern in the right panel.
An edge city is a suburban office center at a highway junction.
The buildings are planned, not self-built on land residents do not own.
Right: density and mixed use around a station.

items.q: Compared with the right panel, how would daily travel in the left panel most likely differ?
options: More car trips, because the station is crowded
Longer trips, because buildings are taller
More trips on foot and by train
About the same, since both have roads

why.correct: In the left panel, homes, shops, jobs and the station are within a short walk, so many trips need no car. In the right panel, every destination is far, so people drive.
options: A busy station means people ride trains instead of driving.
Height puts more destinations close by, so trips get shorter.
Right: nearby destinations and transit cut car trips.
The right panel's layout makes the car the only practical option.

items.q: Which is a criticism often made of neighborhoods like the one in the left panel?
options: They use far more farmland for each home than suburbs do
Rents can rise and price people out
They push most households to own two or more cars
They are built too far from the station to use it

why.correct: Walkable, transit-rich neighborhoods are in demand. When supply is short, rents climb, which can push lower-income households out.
options: Compact building uses less land per home, not more.
Right: rising housing costs are the main criticism.
They reduce the need for cars.
The neighborhood is built around the station.

items.q: Which neighborhood is more walkable, according to the table?
options: Station Square
Oak Hollow
They are equally walkable
The table gives no evidence

why.correct: Station Square has 55% of trips on foot, by bike or by transit and far fewer car kilometers, signs of high walkability.
options: Right: more trips on foot and fewer car kilometers.
Oak Hollow has only 6% of trips without a car.
The two differ sharply on every travel measure.
The trip shares and car kilometers are evidence.

items.q: About how many times more car kilometers does an Oak Hollow household drive each day than a Station Square household?
options: About 2 times
About 10 times
About 46 times
About 5 times

why.correct: 58 divided by 12 is about 4.8, so about 5 times as many.
options: Twice would be 24 km, well below 58.
Ten times would be 120 km.
46 is the difference (58 - 12), not the ratio.
Right: 58 / 12 is about 5.

items.q: Which statement uses the table to give both a benefit and a cost of Station Square's design?
options: Its households drive more each day, and its rents are lower
It has fewer homes per hectare and also lower rents
Less driving, but higher rent
It has more car kilometers per household and fewer homes

why.correct: Less driving (12 vs 58 km) is a benefit; higher rent (\$2,100 vs \$1,500) is a cost. A strong answer names both.
options: Station Square drives less and has higher rents.
It has more homes per hectare (60 vs 8) and higher rents.
Right: one benefit and one cost, both from the table.
It has fewer car kilometers and more homes.

items.q: What is an urban growth boundary?
options: A city's legal border for taxes
A line beyond which building is limited
The edge of a river's floodplain
A border between two countries

why.correct: An urban growth boundary separates land where building is allowed from rural land where it is limited.
options: City limits set taxes and services, not where growth may go.
Right: it steers building inside the line.
A floodplain is a physical feature.
A border between countries is a political boundary.

items.q: The Portland, Oregon, region adopted an urban growth boundary in 1979. Which outcome does this policy aim for?
options: Denser growth inside the line
Faster growth of new suburbs on the farmland around the city
Lower density at the city's center as people move out
More highways built out to distant exurbs and farm towns

why.correct: The boundary steers homes and offices inward, so density rises inside it while farms and forests outside are protected.
options: Right: growth goes up and in, not out.
That is sprawl, which the boundary is meant to limit.
The policy raises density inside the line.
The policy discourages exurban spread.

items.q: Seaside, Florida, begun in the early 1980s, has a grid of narrow streets, houses close to the sidewalk with porches, and a town center within walking distance. Which planning movement does it represent?
options: Urban sprawl
Galactic city
Zone in transition
New Urbanism

why.correct: Designing neighborhoods like older walkable towns, with porches, a street grid and a nearby center, is New Urbanism.
options: Sprawl spreads homes far from shops on wide roads.
The galactic city model describes a whole metro area with edge cities.
The zone in transition belongs to the concentric zone model.
Right: walkable streets and a town center are New Urbanism.

items.q: Boulder, Colorado, has capped the number of new homes built each year since the 1970s. Which effect would critics most expect?
options: Falling home prices as builders compete for buyers
More sprawl on open land inside the city limits
Rising home prices
Less open space protected around the edge of the city

why.correct: If people keep wanting to move in but few homes can be built, prices rise. That is the main criticism of slow-growth caps.
options: A cap limits builders, so competition does not drive prices down.
A cap slows building, so it does not create sprawl inside the city.
Right: limited supply pushes prices up.
The cap is meant to protect open space.

items.q: Critics say smart growth can lead to "de facto segregation". What does that mean here?
options: A city law assigns people to neighborhoods by their income
Separation by income through cost, not law
New highways are built on purpose to divide neighborhoods
Residents choose to live close to the new transit stations

why.correct: De facto means "in fact" rather than by law. If prices rise in desirable areas, lower-income families are separated out by cost alone.
options: A law that assigns people would be de jure, by law.
Right: separation by cost, not by law.
Smart growth usually favors transit over new highways.
Choosing to live near transit is not segregation.

items.q: Copenhagen's 1947 "Finger Plan" lets the city grow outward only along rail lines, like fingers, and keeps green wedges open between them. Which two smart growth ideas does it combine?
options: Transit-oriented growth and protected green space
Edge cities and exurbs
Squatter settlements and market gardens
A primate city and the rank-size rule

why.correct: Growth along rail lines is transit-oriented; the green wedges protect open land, much as a greenbelt does.
options: Right: building follows transit, and green land stays open.
Edge cities and exurbs are products of car-based spread.
Those belong to models of cities in other regions, not to a planning policy.
Those describe city sizes in a country, not a plan for growth.

items.q: Which policies are smart growth tools? Select all that apply.
options: Building apartments above shops near a rail station
Protecting a greenbelt around the city
Building a new highway to farmland 50 km away
Zoning large lots for single houses on the edge

why.correct: Smart growth steers building into compact, connected places and protects land at the edge.
options: Right: mixed use near transit.
Right: a greenbelt limits outward spread.
A highway to distant farmland encourages sprawl.
Large lots at the edge are low-density sprawl.

items.q: Build a statement that gives one benefit and one criticism of a named smart growth policy.

specific.model: Portland's urban growth boundary kept farms and forests close to the city and helped light rail succeed, but critics argue it limited land for homes, so housing costs rose.

place.label: Place and policy
options: Portland's urban growth boundary
Growth rules

why.1: Name a real place and policy: a vague answer earns nothing.

sideA.label: Benefit
options: farms and forests close to the city and helped light rail succeed
drivers from using the city's roads

why.1: The boundary limits where building goes; it does not ban driving.

sideB.label: Criticism
options: critics argue it limited land for homes, so housing costs rose
it caused the city to sprawl onto farmland

why.1: The boundary limits sprawl; the criticism is about housing costs.

why.correct: A strong answer names the place and policy, and speaks of both a benefit and a cost.
